name: Drip
tagline: Send event-triggered ecommerce email from a small user-owned event stream

pricing.notes: Official starting monthly tier for a small contact count.

tiers.name: Email marketing
tiers.limits: Starting plan includes 1-2,500 people; paid customers get unlimited email sends; support included.
tiers.notes: Price scales with active people and email volume.

pricing.freeTierCaps: no free tier; 14-day free trial, no credit card, unlimited emails not available during trial.
pricing.billingTerms: monthly pricing shown; annual plan not verified
pricing.hiddenCosts: Cost rises with active people and email volume; live chat support only on $99/mo+ plans.

verdictSummary: A consolation build is possible, but the paid product's decisive value sits outside a solo rebuild. For Drip, send event-triggered ecommerce email from a small user-owned event stream. The hard boundary is commerce integrations, identity resolution, deliverability, segmentation, and revenue analytics, plus deliverability, growth network, and integrations.
coreLoopDIY: Collect subscribers, send compliant event-triggered ecommerce email from a small user-owned event stream, publish a web archive, and report basic delivery and click events.
whatYouLose: commerce integrations, identity resolution, deliverability, segmentation, and revenue analytics
ongoingBurden: DNS authentication, reputation, bounces, complaints, unsubscribe compliance, templates, queues, analytics, backups, and support
whyPeopleStillPay: People still pay for Drip because newsletter operators pay for inbox placement, growth mechanics, and operational confidence on publication day. The recurring cost buys DNS authentication, reputation, bounces, complaints, unsubscribe compliance, templates, queues, analytics, backups, and support, not just the visible interface.

priorArt.name: Listmonk
priorArt.desc: Mature open-source newsletter and mailing-list manager.

alternatives.name: Dittofeed
alternatives.desc: Cart and product events can trigger branching email journeys; ecommerce integrations are yours to wire.

facts.install: Dittofeed Cloud or Docker Compose/Kubernetes self-host
facts.dataFormat: Self-hosted identity and configuration data lives in PostgreSQL and event/segment data in ClickHouse; optional blob data can use object storage.
facts.gapVsPaid: Dittofeed can trigger journeys from cart and product events, but it lacks Drip's turnkey ecommerce integrations, store-aware reporting, and revenue attribution unless you build them.
facts.setupBlocker: Docker Compose brings Postgres and ClickHouse, but the harder first step is instrumenting product events and connecting an email provider.

alternatives.name: Mautic
alternatives.desc: Tracks behavior and fires campaigns from events; modern ecommerce niceties require integration work.

alternatives.name: Notifuse
alternatives.desc: Event-triggered campaigns and segmentation without contact pricing; store-specific reporting is absent.

facts.install: Notifuse Cloud signup or self-host with Docker
facts.dataFormat: Self-hosted contact, campaign, event, and analytics data lives in PostgreSQL; uploaded assets use S3-compatible storage.
facts.gapVsPaid: Notifuse supports event-triggered campaigns and segmentation, but it does not provide Drip's store-specific dashboards, revenue attribution, or ready-made ecommerce integrations.
facts.setupBlocker: Self-hosting needs Docker, PostgreSQL, object storage, a public domain, and a separately configured SMTP or email API provider.

alternatives.name: Plunk
alternatives.desc: A small event stream can drive conditional email workflows; ecommerce dashboards do not appear by wishing.

facts.dataFormat: Self-hosted data lives in PostgreSQL, queues in Redis, and uploads in bundled MinIO or another S3-compatible store.
facts.gapVsPaid: Plunk can drive conditional email from a small event stream, but it lacks Drip's ecommerce dashboards, product-aware templates, and native store plumbing.
facts.setupBlocker: The self-host path needs Docker, several subdomains, DNS/TLS, and an AWS SES account with credentials and domain verification.

notes: Editorial comparison targets the Email marketing plan and a single-publication newsletter DIY substitute. Recheck price before merge.
prompt:
Build a closest honest personal substitute for Drip in an empty repository.
Use Next.js 15, TypeScript, PostgreSQL, Drizzle ORM, and Amazon SES; do not offer alternative stacks.
The core loop is: collect subscribers, send compliant event-triggered ecommerce email from a small user-owned event stream, publish a web archive, and report basic delivery and click events.
Make the first run work locally with one documented command.
Store all user data locally by default and make export straightforward.
Put secrets in .env, ship .env.example, and never commit credentials.
Implement subscriber import, double opt-in, unsubscribe, suppression, tags, and consent timestamps.
Create a Markdown campaign editor with HTML and plain-text previews.
Queue sends through SES with retries, rate limits, idempotency, and resumable batches.
Process delivery, bounce, complaint, open, and click webhooks without logging message content.
Publish a simple issue archive and subscriber preference page.
Add test sends, seed-list checks, DNS setup guidance, exports, and backups.
Include clear empty, loading, success, and recoverable error states.
Add input validation, safe filenames, and graceful handling of unavailable APIs.
Write focused tests for the core transformation and one end-to-end happy path.
Create a README with setup, architecture, permissions, data location, and backup steps.
Do not add accounts, billing, telemetry, analytics, or a hosted control plane.
Do not claim to reproduce proprietary data, network liquidity, regulated access, or frontier infrastructure.
Deliberately leave out a newsletter recommendation marketplace.
Deliberately leave out ad sales and payment infrastructure.
Deliberately leave out complex lifecycle automation and enterprise deliverability support.
Finish by running the tests and listing the exact commands used.
